concerns.text: The plan proposes using ScanNet (real-world indoor scenes) to evaluate a model trained on 'DreamX-World' (Unreal Engine renders). This introduces a massive domain shift (real vs. synthetic) that acts as a confound. If DreamX-Lite fails, is it due to the geometric prior or the domain mismatch? The plan does not control for this by using a synthetic proxy for DreamX-World or by explicitly modeling the domain shift as a variable.

The plan admits that generating 10-second videos for 50 trajectories on CPU is likely infeasible and proposes reducing rollout length or sample size. Reducing N=50 to N=10-20 destroys the statistical power required for the Wilcoxon test (FR-005) to detect a medium effect size. The methodology relies on a sample size that the hardware constraints explicitly prevent achieving, invalidating the statistical conclusion.

The evaluation relies on recovering camera poses from *generated* videos using COLMAP. If the generative model (especially the ablated 'Lite' version) produces videos with poor 3D consistency or texture, COLMAP will fail to converge. The plan treats 'SfM Failure' as a data point (Infinite MAE), but if the failure rate is high (e.g., >30%), the remaining sample size for the Wilcoxon test becomes too small to draw valid conclusions, creating a selection bias where only 'easy' trajectories are compared.

The plan assumes a 'fixed 4x4 camera pose projection' can replace learned positional encodings (E-PRoPE). However, E-PRoPE likely encodes relative motion and temporal dynamics, not just absolute pose. Injecting only absolute extrinsics may strip the model of necessary temporal priors, causing the 'Lite' model to fail not because geometric priors are insufficient, but because the injection mechanism is incomplete (missing relative/velocity terms). The ablation design does not account for this missing construct.
